hints: Start by finding the cup-shaped structure at the top with a ball of capillaries inside - this is where filtration starts and many other labels relate to it.

Think about where filtrate becomes most concentrated at the end of the journey - which straight tube carries fluid away to the pelvis, and which long loop dips deep down away from the twisted tubules.
Compare the two small blood vessels entering and leaving the capillary ball - one must build up high pressure for filtration, so consider which would be wider on entry.
Podocytes wrap around the filtration capillaries inside the capsule, so B points to the inner wall of the cup, while A points to the final collecting tube that holds urine.
walkthrough:
Orientate Yourself On The Nephron**
Picture filtrate flowing one way: Bowman's capsule at the top in the cortex, then proximal convoluted tubule, then the long loop of Henle dipping down, then distal convoluted tubule, then collecting duct. Blood flows in through the afferent arteriole into the glomerulus, then out through the narrower efferent arteriole.

Place A, B And D Around The Glomerulus**
The ball of capillaries is the glomerulus and the cup around it is Bowman's capsule. Podocytes are the specialised cells of the inner wall of the capsule wrapping the capillaries, so B goes there. The afferent arteriole is the wider incoming vessel that creates high hydrostatic pressure for ultrafiltration, so D goes to the wider of the two vessels entering the capsule. The collecting duct is the straight tube on the right that receives fluid from many nephrons and contains urine, so A goes there.

Place C Deep In The Medulla**
The twisted convoluted tubules stay up in the cortex. Only the loop of Henle and the collecting duct run straight down deep into the medulla to build the salt gradient. So C must point to the loop of Henle or the lower straight part of the collecting duct well below the convoluted region.

Final answer: A - line to collecting duct. B - line to inner layer of Bowman's capsule. C - line to loop of Henle / part of collecting duct below level of convoluted tubules in medulla. D - line to wider vessel entering Bowman's capsule (afferent arteriole).

hints: Remember what selective reabsorption must do - take back all glucose and amino acids plus much of the water and ions from the filtrate into the blood, so think what membrane features would speed up uptake.
Glucose cannot diffuse back on its own - think how it is linked to sodium ion movement and what type of membrane protein would allow this.
Moving sodium out of the cell against its gradient needs energy - think which organelle must be plentiful and where the pumps sit on the cell membrane.
If fluid leaked between cells it would bypass control - think what seal between cells forces everything to go through the selective cell membranes.
walkthrough:
Increase Uptake Area With Microvilli**
The apical membrane facing the tubule lumen is folded into a dense brush border of microvilli. This hugely increases surface area for carrier proteins and channels, so diffusion and cotransport of glucose, amino acids, ions and water back into the cell is much faster.

Cotransport Useful Solutes With Sodium**
Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed by sodium-linked cotransporter proteins in the apical membrane. Sodium moves down its concentration gradient into the cell and drags glucose or amino acids with it, allowing complete recovery of these valuable solutes from the filtrate.

Power Sodium Pumping With Mitochondria And Folded Base**
The basal membrane next to the blood is highly folded to hold many sodium-potassium pumps. These pumps actively transport $Na^{+}$ out of the cell into tissue fluid using ATP. The many mitochondria in these cells supply that ATP by aerobic respiration, maintaining the low intracellular $Na^{+}$ gradient that drives cotransport.

Force Control Through Cells With Tight Junctions**
Adjacent cells are joined by tight junctions near the lumen. This seals the gaps between cells so filtrate cannot leak through uncontrolled. All reabsorbed substances must pass through the selective cell surface membranes, which is why reabsorption is selective.

Final answer: Any four: microvilli / brush border gives large surface area for reabsorption; cotransporter proteins for uptake of glucose / amino acids with $Na^{+}$; tight junctions between cells prevent leakage between cells so substances pass through cells; many mitochondria provide ATP for active transport of $Na^{+}$ out; highly folded basal membrane houses many sodium-potassium pumps.
